messages.subject: Trap Saturation vs Trap Interference
parts:
Hi Murray,

we previously corresponded on what I had perceived as a problem with trap saturation (which I have defined as less than 16% trap availability on average across 6 occasions) on 7 of 24 gridsI have established to monitor Bandicoots. The question related to pooling g0 from grids with different levels of saturation.  Following your advice I estimated g0 and sigma for those 7 grids separately to the remaining (unsaturated) grids. Surprisingly g0 was higher on the saturated grids compared to the unsaturated grids (0.041 vs 0.0176 for males and 0.102 vs 0.0419 for females) and sigma was lower  (72.86 vs 78.4 for males and 52.21 vs 70.51).  I  also found that trap "saturation" wasn't necessarily a function of increased density eg density ranged between 0.8 and 2.2 Bandicoots per Ha on saturated grids and between 0.86 and 2.1 Bandicoots per ha on unsaturated grids.  Further investigation of the data indicates that many of the traps had been interfered with or malfunctioned - that is I had scored them as "Open no Bait" or "Closed no Animal".  Interference results from increasingly interested Bandicoots (because they have a very strong learned response with g0 increasing tenfold) or from other species (namely possums and bettongs).  Malfunctioning traps are caused by a variety of factors, some of them avoidable.  If saturation was solely a function of increasing density I would expect a negative bias in g0 as demonstrated by yourself and more recently Distiller and Borchers.  But does the increase in g0 in my case suggests something else is at play?  If the traps have been rendered "unavailable" due to interference (whether they had the potential to capture a Bandicoot or not at the start of an occasion)  should I then exclude them from that occasion - this gets very complicated as different traps are impacted across different occasions.  Seems to me that this scenario would explain an increase in g0 where trap saturation isn't really a function of increasing trap occupation (or increased density).  Of course habitat difference across the 24 locations where I have established grids may also explain differences in g0 and sigma. 

Thanks

Roy

messages.author: 118cea91a1619106
messages.subject: Re: Trap Saturation vs Trap Interference
parts:
Hi Roy 
There could be a lot going on here we can't see, but...
Given that estimates of sigma are not much affected by trap saturation, it seems quite plausible that animals on your more saturated sites have smaller home ranges. Everything else being equal, this will lead to lower g0 (e.g. Efford & Mowat 2014 Ecology 95: 1341), which might be sufficient to explain the g0 effect you describe, or there could be other systematic habitat differences as you say. However, I am a bit doubtful this explanation is enough. Another contributing factor might be that the process(es) disabling traps act diurnally after the bandicoots have had their go at the traps, so the saturation is more apparent than real. I don't recommend treating traps that malfunctioned as 'not set' unless there was a clear mechanical problem that meant they were doomed to never catch an animal. It does seem wise to stratify by saturation, unless there is a better model for variation in g0 and sigma.
I agree this needs more thought, and it's not an uncommon problem - it was often the case in our brushtail possum studies that almost no traps remained unsprung
Murray
